**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

I.

The first time I realized words had weight was when my father told me, *"You’re not trying hard enough."* I was eight, sitting at the kitchen table with a math worksheet smeared with eraser dust. The numbers blurred together, and my fingers ached from gripping the pencil too tight. His voice wasn’t loud—it didn’t need to be. The words settled in my chest like a stone dropped into a well, and I’ve been carrying them ever since.

Words are supposed to be light, aren’t they? Just air pushed through vocal cords, shapes on a page. But some of them lodge in you. They calcify. They become part of the skeleton of who you are.

II.

I used to think silence was the absence of words, but now I know it’s just the space between them—the breath before the storm, the pause before the confession. My mother was a master of silence. She could go days without speaking, not out of anger, but because she understood that some things couldn’t be said without breaking. The unspoken was its own language in our house. A slammed door. A plate left unwashed in the sink. The way she’d stare out the window when my father’s car pulled into the driveway, her fingers tightening around her coffee mug.

I inherited her silence, but not her grace. Mine is jagged, full of things I swallow until they cut me from the inside.

III.

There’s a myth that writers are people who have something to say. That’s not true. Writers are people who are afraid of what will happen if they *don’t* say it. We’re all just trying to exorcise the ghosts before they strangle us.

I write because the alternative is screaming. I write because one day, I opened my mouth and nothing came out, and I realized I had been holding my breath for years.

IV.

Do you ever think about how strange it is that we trust words at all? They’re slippery things. *"I love you"* can mean forever or it can mean *for now*. *"It’s not you, it’s me"* is a lie wrapped in politeness. *"We should talk"* is never about the weather.

Language is a contract we all agree to, even though we know it’s flawed. We pretend that words mean the same thing to everyone, but they don’t. *"Home"* to one person is a house with a white picket fence. To another, it’s the backseat of a car. To me, it’s the smell of rain on hot pavement and the way my grandmother’s hands looked when she peeled an orange.

V.

I had a professor in college who said, *"All writing is an act of translation."* At the time, I thought he meant translating ideas into words. Now I think he meant translating the chaos inside us into something that won’t destroy us.

I try to translate my rage into poems. My grief into stories. My love into letters I never send. Some things resist translation. Some things are better left in the original language of the heart, where they can’t be misinterpreted.

VI.

Have you ever noticed how the most important conversations happen in moving vehicles? Maybe it’s because you can’t look each other in the eye. Maybe it’s because the hum of the engine drowns out the sound of your own voice, makes it easier to say the hard things.

My best friend told me she was pregnant in the passenger seat of my car, staring out the window as we idled at a red light. My brother told me he was gay on a midnight drive with the radio turned low. I told my first love I couldn’t stay with him while we sat in a parking lot, the steering wheel digging into my palms.

There’s something about motion that makes the truth feel safer. As if we can outrun the consequences.

VII.

I used to believe in the power of words to change things. Now I’m not so sure. You can say *"I’m sorry"* a thousand times, but it won’t unbreak what’s broken. You can write *"This is who I am"* in bold letters, but some people will still misread you.

Words are tools, but they’re not magic. They can build bridges or burn them. They can heal or they can wound. But they can’t make someone love you. They can’t bring back the dead. They can’t rewrite history.

VIII.

I think about the words I’ve lost. The ones I meant to say but didn’t. The ones I said too loudly, too carelessly. The ones that got stuck in my throat like fishbones.

There’s a Japanese word, *"kuyashii,"* which means the bitter feeling of regret after losing something you could have won. I feel *kuyashii* about all the words I’ve wasted. All the words I’ve hoarded. All the words I’ve let other people define for me.

IX.

If I had 1,000 words left, what would I do with them?

Would I spend them on love letters to people who are already gone?
Would I waste them on arguments with strangers on the internet?
Would I save them for my future self, a message in a bottle tossed into the sea of time?

Or would I use them to say the things I’ve been too afraid to say out loud?

*I miss you.*
*I don’t know how to fix this.*
*I’m trying my best, but my best isn’t always enough.*
*I forgive you.*
*Please forgive me.*

X.

The older I get, the more I believe in the power of fewer words. Not silence, exactly—just precision. A surgeon’s scalpel, not a sledgehammer. *"I love you"* instead of *"I think I might possibly have feelings for you under the right circumstances."* *"No"* instead of *"I’m not sure, maybe, let me think about it."*

But then there are the moments when only a flood will do. When the dam breaks and all the words come rushing out, messy and raw and true. Those are the moments that change things. Those are the moments that matter.

XI.

I don’t know how to end this. Maybe that’s the point.

Words don’t have to be perfect. They just have to be *yours*. They just have to mean something, to someone, even if that someone is only you.

So here’s what I’ll leave you with:

The world is full of noise. But your voice—no matter how shaky, no matter how quiet—deserves to be heard.

Use your words. Even when they’re heavy. Especially when they’re heavy.

Because in the end, they’re all we’ve got.
